title: Scoping an MVP AI Feature

thumbnail.headline: Design the Wrong Path
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a flow diagram splitting into one teal happy path and four orange failure branches, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Design the Wrong Path
slide.body: Flow: one teal happy path and four branches labelled wrong, unsure, should not answer, unavailable. Small tag: AI Product Management · Lesson 5.

production_notes: [VERSION] Figma and FigJam free-plan limits must be checked before recording (exercise tool).
Nour Hassan and the online marketplace in Egypt are hypothetical; no real marketplace interface or logo. Giza is mentioned only as a place in a buyer question.
The phone mock-ups on the slides show reply drafts in both Arabic and English; any Arabic text on screen needs a native-speaker check and Noto Sans Arabic.

Hook.voiceover: Every AI feature has two user journeys: the one where the AI is right, and the one where it is wrong. Most teams design the first one carefully, and discover the second one after launch. Today, we design both on day one.
Hook.on_screen_text: Two journeys, both designed on day one

Explain.voiceover: You now have a top idea. The next step is to scope it. An AI minimum viable product should be narrow, and four limits help. In the last lesson, a narrower scope lowered the error cost. Now we make that concrete.

One user: a single group with a clear need, such as new sellers, not all users. One task: one judgement task done well. A human in the loop: in the first version, a person approves the output before it has an effect. And a clear fallback: the product must still work when the AI is unsure, fails or is switched off.

slide.title: Four limits for an AI MVP
slide.body: 1. One user · 2. One task · 3. A human in the loop · 4. A clear non-AI fallback

Explain.voiceover: Then design the experience for errors as carefully as the happy path. Ask four questions. When the AI is wrong, how does the user notice and correct it? When it is unsure, what does the user see? When it should not answer, what message appears? And when it is unavailable, what is the normal path?

slide.title: Four failure paths
slide.body: Happy path in teal; four branches: Wrong → notice and correct · Unsure → fewer or no suggestions · Should not answer → clear message and next step · Unavailable → normal non-AI path

Explain.voiceover: For the unsure case, your team can often use a confidence score or a set of rules to decide when to show nothing at all.

slide.title: When to show nothing
slide.body: Confidence score or rules → threshold line → above: show suggestions · below: ask a clarifying question, show fewer, or show none.

Explain.voiceover: Also design a feedback loop: a simple way for users to say this was helpful, or this was wrong. This becomes your first real evaluation data. Keep it light, with one tap, so users actually use it.

slide.title: Feedback loop
slide.body: AI output → user taps 'helpful' or 'wrong' → feedback data → back to the team. Label: your first real evaluation data.

Explain.voiceover: Here is a way to picture it. A new pilot does not fly passengers alone on the first day. They fly one route, with a senior pilot next to them, and they practise emergency procedures before normal flights.
Explain.broll_prompt: A young South Asian woman pilot in the co-pilot seat of a flight simulator follows a checklist while an older Black male captain beside her points to the controls and nods; slow push-in from a wide cockpit shot to a medium two-shot; cool blue instrument light with warm side light; cinematic, realistic, shallow depth of field; 7 seconds; no readable text, no airline names, no logos.
Explain.on_screen_text: One route, a senior pilot beside you

Explain.voiceover: An AI MVP flies one route, with a human next to it, and its emergency procedures are designed before launch.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see an example. Nour Hassan is a PM at a hypothetical online marketplace in Egypt, where people sell used furniture and electronics. Sellers get many buyer questions, such as can you deliver to Giza, and slow replies lose sales.
Demonstrate.stock_query: person replying to messages on smartphone

Demonstrate.voiceover: The first idea was an AI assistant that handles all buyer conversations. Nour narrows it. The user is sellers with fewer than twenty listings, who reply from their phones. The task is to suggest up to three short reply drafts, in Arabic or English to match the buyer. The seller taps, edits and sends. Nothing is sent automatically.

slide.title: Narrowing the scope
slide.body: Before: AI assistant handles all buyer conversations. After: User = sellers with fewer than 20 listings · Task = up to 3 reply drafts in Arabic or English · Human = seller taps, edits, sends · Fallback = normal empty reply box.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now the failure paths. Wrong: a suggestion makes a delivery promise the seller never made. So suggestions never include prices, dates or promises unless they come from the listing. Unsure: the message is unclear. So show one neutral suggestion, asking the buyer to say more, or show none.

slide.title: Failure paths 1 and 2
slide.body: Wrong: invented delivery promise → no prices, dates or promises unless from the listing. Unsure: unclear message → one neutral suggestion ('Could you tell me more?') or none.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Should not answer: the message contains abuse or asks for personal data. So there are no suggestions, and a report this message link appears. Unavailable: the normal reply box appears, with no error message for the seller. In each case, the seller always knows what to do next.

slide.title: Failure paths 3 and 4
slide.body: Should not answer: abuse or personal data request → no suggestions + 'Report this message' link. Unavailable: normal reply box, no error shown.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Every suggestion has a small not useful button. Nour will use those taps, and whether sellers edit suggestions or send them unchanged, as early quality signals. These signals cost almost nothing to collect, and they show real use from the first day.

slide.title: Early quality signals
slide.body: Phone mock-up with three reply drafts and a small 'Not useful' button → signals: 'Not useful' taps · edited vs sent unchanged.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is thinking a human in the loop makes errors unimportant. Busy users stop checking carefully when suggestions are usually right. So make errors easy to see. For example, keep promises and numbers out of the drafts, and do not rely only on the user's attention.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, scope an AI MVP to one user, one task, a human in the loop and a clear fallback. Second, design four failure paths: wrong, unsure, should not answer and unavailable. Third, build a simple feedback signal into the first version, because it becomes your first real evaluation data.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. One user, one task, human in the loop, fallback. 2. Four failure paths. 3. Build in a feedback signal from day one.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, sketch the happy path and the four failure paths for your feature in Figma or FigJam. Keep the board, because you will reuse it in the capstone. It takes about thirty minutes. In the next lesson, we look at data needs, and what your feature learns from. See you there.
